It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata al-Khurasani, Zayd ibn Aslam, and others: ﴿When he reached the age of exertion with him⟩ means: he grew up, became capable, and was able to do what his father did of striving and working. ﴿When he reached the age of exertion with him, he said: "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think."⟩ 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: The dreams of the prophets are revelation. Then he recited this verse: ﴿He said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think."⟩

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated to us: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn al-Junayd narrated to us, Abu 'Abd al-Malik al-Karandi narrated to us, Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from Isra'il ibn Yunus, from Simak, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dreams of the prophets in sleep are revelation." This is not in any of the Six Books by this route. [Al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (12/6) narrated it by another route from Simak: he narrated it through al-Firyabi, from Sufyan, from Simak ibn Harb, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas.]

He informed his son of this only so that it would be easier for him, and to test his patience, endurance, and resolve from his youth in obeying Allah the Exalted and obeying his father.

﴿He said, "O my father, do what you are commanded."⟩ That is: carry out what Allah has commanded you regarding my slaughter. ﴿"You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient."⟩ That is: I will be patient and will seek reward for that with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He spoke the truth, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, in what he promised. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet. And he used to enjoin on his people prayer and zakah, and he was pleasing to his Lord.⟩ [Maryam: 54–55]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when they both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead⟩ means: when both of them bore witness [to the faith] and remembered Allah the Exalted, Ibrahim [prepared] for the slaughter, and the son [prepared] for the witness of death. It is also said: ﴿aslama﴾ [in the sense] of [yastaslima] and yanqada: they surrendered and submitted. Ibrahim complied with Allah's command, and Isma'il obeyed Allah and his father. This was said by Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Ibn Ishaq, and others.

The meaning of ﴿and he put him down upon his forehead⟩ is that he threw him onto his face so that he could slaughter him from the nape of his neck, and so that he would not see his face at the time of slaughter, to make it easier for him. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, and Qatadah said: ﴿and he put him down upon his forehead⟩ means: he laid him down on his face.

Imam Ahmad said: Surayj [in manuscript A: Shurayj] and Yunus narrated to us, both saying: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Abu 'Asim al-Ghanawi, from Abu al-Tufayl [in manuscript T: "with its chain"], from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: When Ibrahim was commanded with the rites (al-manasik) [in manuscript A: "When Allah commanded Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with the rites"], Satan confronted him at the place of running (al-sa'y), so he raced him, and Ibrahim outran him. Then Jibril took him to Jamrat al-'Aqabah, and Satan confronted him there, so he pelted him with seven pebbles until he departed. Then he confronted him at the middle jamrah, and he pelted him with seven pebbles. Then he laid him down upon his forehead, and Isma'il was wearing a white shirt. He said to him: "O father, I have no garment to be shrouded in except this one, so take it off so that you may shroud me in it." He began to take it off, and he was called from behind: ﴿"O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision."⟩ Ibrahim turned, and behold, there was a white ram with curled horns and beautiful eyes. Ibn 'Abbas said: We used to follow that kind of ram.

He mentioned the complete hadith at length in "al-Manasik." [al-Musnad (1/297)] Then Ahmad narrated it at length from Yunus, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from 'Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr [in manuscript T: "with its chain"], from Ibn 'Abbas, and he mentioned something similar, except that he said: "Ishaq." [al-Musnad (1/306)] So there are two reports from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the identity of the one to be sacrificed, and the more apparent from him is Isma'il, for reasons that will come later.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, from al-Hasan ibn Dinar, from Qatadah, from Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.⟩ He said: A ram came out to him from Paradise, which had grazed for forty autumns before that. Ibrahim sent his son away and followed the ram, and it led him to the first jamrah, and he pelted it with seven pebbles, and it escaped from him there. It came to the middle jamrah, and he brought it out there, and he pelted it with seven pebbles, and then it escaped. He caught up with it at the greatest jamrah, and he pelted it with seven pebbles, and brought it out there. Then he took it and brought it to the place of sacrifice (al-manhar) at Mina, and slaughtered it. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Ibn 'Abbas, the head of the ram was indeed hanging by its horns on the gutter of the Ka'bah from the beginning of Islam, and it had dried out, meaning: it had become dry.

'Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, who informed us, al-Qasim said: Abu Hurayrah and Ka'b met. Abu Hurayrah began to narrate from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ka'b began to narrate from the scriptures. Abu Hurayrah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every prophet has a supplication that is answered, and I have kept my supplication as an intercession for my nation on the Day of Resurrection." Ka'b said to him: "Did you hear this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "Yes." He said: "May my father and mother be your ransom, or: may his father and mother be his ransom. Shall I not tell you about Ibrahim (peace be upon him)? When he was shown the sacrifice of his son Ishaq, Satan said: 'If I do not tempt these people at this [moment], I will never tempt them.' So Ibrahim went out with his son to sacrifice him. Satan went and entered upon Sarah and said: 'Where did Ibrahim take your son?' She said: 'He went out with him for some need of his.' He said: 'He did not go out for a need; he took him only to sacrifice him.' She said: 'And why would he sacrifice him?' He said: 'He claims that his Lord commanded him to do so.' She said: 'Then he has done well to obey his Lord.' Satan went after the two of them and said to the boy: 'Where is your father taking you?' He said: 'For some need of his.' He said: 'He does not take you for a need; he takes you only to sacrifice you.' He said: 'And why would he sacrifice me?' He said: 'He claims that his Lord commanded him to do so.' He said: 'By Allah, if Allah has commanded him to do so, then he will certainly do it.' So he despaired of him, and he left him and caught up with Ibrahim, and said: 'Where did you go out with your son?' He said: 'For a need.' He said: 'You did not go out with him for a need; you went out with him only to sacrifice him.' He said: 'And why would I sacrifice him?' He said: 'You claim that your Lord commanded you to do so.' He said: 'By Allah, if my Lord has commanded me to do so, I will certainly do it.' So he left him and despaired of being obeyed."

Ibn Jarir narrated it from Yunus, from Ibn Wahb, from Yunus ibn Yazid, from Ibn Shihab, that 'Amr ibn Abi Sufyan ibn Usayd [in manuscript A: "Asad"] ibn Jariyah al-Thaqafi informed him that Ka'b said to Abu Hurayrah ... and he mentioned it at length, and at its end he said: Allah revealed to Ishaq: "I have given you a supplication, and I will answer you in it." Ishaq said: "O Allah, I ask You to accept from me: any servant who meets You from among the first and the last, who does not associate anything with You, admit him into Paradise."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated to us: My father narrated to us, Muhammad ibn al-Wazir al-Dimashqi narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam narrated to us, from his father, from 'Ata ibn Yasar [in manuscript T: "and he narrated with his chain"], from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) [addition from manuscript T], who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah gave me the choice between forgiving half of my nation and between my keeping my intercession hidden. So I hid my intercession, and I hoped that it would be [an expiation] for my nation as a whole [in manuscript A: 'that it would be more general']. And had it not been for what the righteous servant (Ibrahim) had preceded me in, I would have hastened my supplication for it. Indeed, when Allah relieved Ishaq of the distress of the slaughter, it was said to him: 'O Ishaq, ask, and you will be given.' He said: 'As for Him in whose hand is my soul, I will hasten it before the whisperings of Satan. O Allah, whoever dies without associating anything with You, forgive him and admit him into Paradise.'"

This is a hadith, a strange and rejected (munkar) narration, narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Awsat (no. 3603) and by Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil (4/272) through al-Walid ibn Muslim, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, with it. Ibn Abi Hatim also mentioned it in al-'Ilal (2/219) and said: "I asked my father, and he said: 'This is a munkar hadith.'" 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam is weak in narration. I fear that there is an interpolated addition (mudraja) in the hadith, namely his saying: "Indeed Allah, when He relieved Ishaq..." to the end. And Allah knows best. So if this is preserved, the more likely reading is that the context is about Isma'il, and they distorted it to Ishaq out of envy, as has already been mentioned. Otherwise, the rites of pilgrimage and the sacrifices are only located at Mina, in the land of Makkah, where Isma'il, not Ishaq, was [peace be upon them both]. Ishaq was in the land of Canaan in the region of the Levant.

* *

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ That is: the purpose of your vision has been achieved by your laying your son down for slaughter.

Al-Suddi and others mentioned that he drew the knife across his neck, but it did not cut anything; rather, a plate of copper came between the knife and him. Then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was called at that moment: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision.﴾

* *

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ That is: thus do We turn away from those who obey Us hardships and calamities, and We make for them, in their affair, relief and a way out, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Allah has already set for everything a decree.﴾ [At-Talaq: 2-3]

A group of scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) used this verse and the story as evidence for the validity of naskh (abrogation, the lifting of a previously prescribed ruling by a later one) before the command could be carried out, contrary to a group of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school). The proof from this is clear: Allah the Exalted prescribed for Ibrahim the slaughter of his son, then abrogated it for him and turned it into a ransom. The primary purpose of the original command was to reward the Friend (Khalil) for his patience in the face of slaughtering his son and his determination to do so. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial.﴾ That is: the evident and manifest test, in that he was commanded to slaughter his son, and he hastened to that, submitting to the command of Allah and obeying Him. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant].﴾ [An-Najm: 37]

* *

And His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ Sufyan al-Thawri narrated from Jabir al-Ju'fi, from Abu al-Tufayl, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾: he said: "With a white ram, with beautiful eyes and curved horns, which had been tied to a samurah tree." Abu al-Tufayl said: "They found it tied to a samurah tree on Thabir."

Al-Thawri also said, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman ibn Khuthaym, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A ram that had grazed in Paradise for forty autumns."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Saffar narrated to us, Dawud al-'Attar narrated to us, from Ibn Khuthaym, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The rock that is in Mina at the base of Thabir is the rock on which Ibrahim slaughtered the ransom for his son. There descended upon it from Thabir a ram, with beautiful eyes and curved horns, which bleated; so he slaughtered it. It is the ram that Adam's son (Qabil/Habil) offered, and it was accepted from him. It was kept stored until Ishaq was ransomed with it."

It is also narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "The ram used to graze in Paradise until Thabir split open for it, and it had red wool on it."

From al-Hasan al-Basri: the name of Ibrahim's ram was Jarir.

Ibn Jurayj said: 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "He slaughtered it at al-Maqam." Mujahid said: "He slaughtered it at Mina, at the place of sacrifice (al-mantar)." Hushaym narrated from Sayyar, from 'Ikrimah, that Ibn 'Abbas once issued a fatwa to the one who had vowed to sacrifice himself, instructing him to sacrifice one hundred camels. Then he said afterwards: "Had I issued him a fatwa to sacrifice a ram, it would have sufficed him to slaughter a ram, for Allah the Exalted said in His Book: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾" The sound view, which most scholars hold, is that he was ransomed with a ram. Al-Thawri narrated from a man, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾: he said: "A wa'l (a mountain goat)."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, from al-Hasan, that he used to say: "Isma'il was ransomed only with a male antelope (tays min al-aruwa), which descended upon him from Thabir."

Imam Ahmad has also said: Sufyan narrated to us, Mansur narrated to us, from his maternal uncle Musafi', from Safiyyah bint Shaybah, who said: "A woman from the Banu Sulaym, who had given birth to most of the people of our household, informed me that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent for 'Uthman ibn Talhah" (and at one point she said: "She asked 'Uthman: 'Why did the Prophet ﷺ call you?' He said: 'He said: "I had seen the two horns of the ram when I entered the House, and I forgot to order you to cover them. So cover them, for it is not fitting that there be anything in the House that distracts the one who prays."'") Sufyan said: "The two horns of the ram remained hanging in the House until the House burned, and they burned." [Al-Musnad (4/68)]

This is independent evidence that it was Isma'il, peace be upon him, for the Quraysh inherited the two horns of the ram with which Ibrahim was ransomed, from predecessor to successor, generation after generation, until Allah sent His Messenger ﷺ.

A section on the narrations transmitted from the early generations (al-salaf) regarding who the sacrificed son was:

Mention of those who said: it was Ishaq [peace be upon him]:

Hamzah al-Zayyat narrated from Abu Maysarah, may Allah have mercy on him, who said: Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to the king to his face: "Do you desire to eat with me? I am—by Allah—Yusuf ibn Ya'qub, the Prophet of Allah, son of Ishaq, the one who was sacrificed by Allah, son of Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah."

Al-Thawri said, from Abu Sinan, from Ibn Abi al-Hudhayl: that Yusuf, peace be upon him, said the same to the king.

Sufyan al-Thawri said, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, from his father, who said: "Musa said: 'O Lord, they say: "O God of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub." Why do they say that?' He said: 'Ibrahim never once preferred anything over Me without My choosing him over it. As for Ishaq, he gave himself to Me for slaughter, and he was more generous than that. As for Ya'qub, whenever I increased him in trial, he increased in good opinion of Me.'"

Shu'bah said, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, who said: A man boasted in the presence of Ibn Mas'ud, saying: "I am so-and-so son of so-and-so, the son of noble elders." 'Abd Allah said: "That is Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq, the one sacrificed by Allah, son of Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah [may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all]."

This is sound up to Ibn Mas'ud. Likewise, 'Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was Ishaq, and from his father al-'Abbas and from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib the same. Likewise said 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Abu Maysarah, Zayd ibn Aslam, 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, al-Zuhri, al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, Makhul, 'Uthman ibn Hadir, al-Suddi, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu al-Hudhayl, and Ibn Sabit. This is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir. His narration from Ka'b al-Ahbar that it was Ishaq has already been mentioned.

Thus Ibn Ishaq narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Sufyan ibn al-'Ala', ibn Jariyah, from Abu Hurayrah, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, that he said: "It was Ishaq." [Narrated by al-Tabari in his tafsir (23/52)]

And all of these reports, and Allah knows best, derive from Ka'b al-Ahbar. For when he embraced Islam during the caliphate of 'Umar, he began to narrate to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, from his books. 'Umar would sometimes listen to him, so people became lenient about listening to what he had, and they transmitted from him both its worthless and its valuable parts, while this Ummah—and Allah knows best—has no need for a single letter of what he had. Al-Baghawi has recorded this view, that it was Ishaq, from 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, and al-'Abbas, and from the Successors (tabi'un): Ka'b al-Ahbar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Masruq, 'Ikrimah, Muqatil, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, and al-Suddi. He said: "And it is one of the two reports from Ibn 'Abbas." [Ma'alim al-Tanzil of al-Baghawi (7/46)]

A hadith has been transmitted on this subject—if it were established, we would act upon it wholeheartedly, but its chain is not sound. Ibn Jarir said:

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, Zayd ibn Hubab narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Dinar, from 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, from al-Hasan, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, from the Prophet ﷺ, in a hadith he mentioned, who said: "He was Ishaq." [Tafsir al-Tabari (23/52)]

In its chain there are two weak narrators: al-Hasan ibn Dinar al-Basri, who is abandoned (matruk), and 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, whose narrations are munkar. Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it from his father, from Muslim ibn Ibrahim, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, with it, raised to the Prophet ﷺ, and that he said: "He was Ishaq." Then he said: "It was also narrated by Mubarak ibn Fadalah, from al-Hasan, from al-Ahnaf, from al-'Abbas, as his own statement (mawquf), and this is more likely and more sound."

[Mention of the reports stating that it was Isma'il, peace be upon him, which is the sound and definitive view]

The narration from Ibn 'Abbas that it was Ishaq has already been mentioned. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Amir al-Sha'bi, Yusuf ibn Mihran, Mujahid, 'Ata', and others said, from Ibn 'Abbas, that it was Isma'il, peace be upon him.

Ibn Jarir said: Yunus narrated to me, Ibn Wahb informed us, 'Amr ibn Qays informed me, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "The one ransomed was Isma'il, peace be upon him. The Jews claim that it was Ishaq, but the Jews are lying." [Tafsir al-Tabari (23/52)]

Israil narrated from Thawr, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The sacrificed one was Isma'il."

Ibn Abi Najih said, from Mujahid: "It was Isma'il." Yusuf ibn Mihran also said the same.

Al-Sha'bi said: "It was Isma'il, peace be upon him, and I have seen the two horns of the ram in the Ka'bah."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from al-Hasan ibn Dinar and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, from al-Hasan al-Basri, that he had no doubt about this: that the one of Ibrahim's two sons he was commanded to sacrifice was Isma'il.

Ibn Ishaq said: "I heard Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi say: 'The one whom Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice from among his two sons was Isma'il. We find that in the Book of Allah, for when Allah finished the story of the one sacrificed from Ibrahim's two sons, He said: ﴿And We gave him good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ Allah says: ﴿So We gave her good news of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub.﴾ That means: a son and a grandson. So He would not have commanded him to sacrifice Ishaq when He had promised him through him what He promised. The one He commanded to be sacrificed was none other than Isma'il.'"

Ibn Ishaq said, on the authority of Buraydah ibn Sufyan ibn Farwah al-Aslami, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, that he [Muhammad ibn Ka'b] told them that he mentioned this to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz when he was caliph and [Muhammad] was with him in al-Sham. Umar said to him, "This is a matter I had never considered, and I indeed see it as you have said." Then he sent for a man who was with him in al-Sham, who had been a Jew, then embraced Islam and whose Islam was good, and who thought of himself as one of their scholars. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asked him about this. (Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "I was with Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz.") Umar said to him, "Which of Abraham's two sons was he commanded to sacrifice?" He said, "Isma'il, by Allah, O Commander of the Faithful. The Jews indeed know this, but they envy you, the Arab people, that your father is the one to whom this occurred by the command of Allah, and the virtue Allah mentioned of him for his patience in what he was commanded. So they deny it and claim it was Isaac, because Isaac is their father. Allah knows best which of them it was. Both were pure, good, and obedient to Allah, Mighty and Majestic."* [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (23/54).]

'Abd Allah ibn al-Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "I asked my father about the one who was sacrificed: who was he? Isma'il or Isaac?" He said, "Isma'il." He mentioned this in the Kitab al-Zuhd (Book of Asceticism).

Ibn Abi Hatim said: "And I heard my father say: 'The correct view is that the one sacrificed was Isma'il, peace be upon him.'" He said: "It is also reported from Ali, Ibn Umar, Abu Hurayrah, Abu al-Tufayl, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali, and Abu Salih, that they said: 'The one sacrificed was Isma'il.'"

Al-Baghawi said in his Tafsir: "This is the view of Abd Allah ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Suddi, al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and al-Kalbi. It is also a narration from Ibn Abbas. He also reported it from Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala'."* [Ma'alim al-Tanzil of al-Baghawi (7/47).]

Ibn Jarir narrated a strange hadith on this. He said: Muhammad ibn Ammar al-Razi told me, Isma'il ibn Ubayd ibn Abi Karimah told us, Umar ibn Abd al-Rahim al-Khattabi told us, from Ubayd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Utbi (a descendant of Utbah ibn Abi Sufyan), from his father, who said: Abd Allah ibn Sa'id told me, from al-Sunabihi, who said: "We were with Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, and the people mentioned the sacrificed one: Isma'il or Isaac? He said: 'You have fallen into [a matter] of which the knowledgeable one knows. We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when a man came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, give me from what Allah has granted you, O son of the two sacrificed ones!" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed. It was said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, who are the two sacrificed ones?" He said: "When Abd al-Muttalib was commanded to dig Zamzam, he vowed to Allah that if Allah made its matter easy for him, he would sacrifice one of his sons. The arrow fell upon Abd Allah, but his maternal uncles prevented it and said: 'Ransom your son with a hundred camels.' So he ransomed him with a hundred camels. The second [sacrificed one] was Isma'il.'"*[Tafsir al-Tabari (23/54).]

This is a very strange hadith. Al-Umawi also narrated it in his Maghazi: some of our companions told us, Isma'il ibn Ubayd ibn Abi Karimah informed us, Umar ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Qurashi told us, Ubayd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Utbi (a descendant of Utbah ibn Abi Sufyan) told us, Abd Allah ibn Sa'id told us, al-Sunabihi told us, who said: "We attended the gathering of Mu'awiyah, and the people discussed Isma'il and Isaac," and he mentioned it. So I copied it this way from a faulty copy [in the text: "from a copy of such-and-such, and Allah knows best"].

Ibn Jarir based his preference that the sacrificed one was Isaac on the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾. He took this good news to be the good news of Isaac in the words: ﴿And they gave him good news of a knowing boy﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:28]. He answered the good news of Ya'qub (Jacob) by saying that he had reached the age of striving with him, meaning working. It is possible that children had also been born to him with Ya'qub. He said: As for the two horns that were hanging in the Ka'bah, it is permissible that they were brought from the lands of al-Sham. He said: It has already been mentioned that some people held that he sacrificed Isaac there. This is what he relied upon in his Tafsir, but what he held is neither a sound doctrine nor a binding one; rather it is very far-fetched. What Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi used as evidence that it was Isma'il is more firmly established, more sound, and stronger. Allah knows best.* [Imam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, examined this issue in his Fatawa. See the references in the General Index (36/32).]

* *

His words: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Since the good news of the sacrificed one, who is Isma'il, was mentioned earlier, He followed it with the mention of the good news of his brother Isaac. I have mentioned this in the commentary on Surah Hud and Surah al-Hijr.* [Surah Hud, verse 71; Surah al-Hijr, verse 53.]

* *

His words: ﴿nabiyyan﴾ (a prophet) is a circumstantial clause (hal) that is anticipated, meaning: a prophet from among the righteous will come from him.

Ibn Jarir said: Ya'qub told me, Ibn Ulayyah told us, from Dawud, from Ikrimah, who said: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The sacrificed one was Isaac." He said: As for His words, ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾, he said: "He gave him good news of his prophethood." He said: As for His words, ﴿And We bestowed upon him out of Our mercy his brother Aaron, a prophet﴾ [Maryam 19:53], he said: "Aaron was older than Musa, but the meaning is: He granted him his prophethood."

And Ibn Abd al-A'la told us, al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman told us, he said: "I heard Dawud narrate, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, concerning this verse: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾," he said: "He gave him good news of him as a prophet only when Allah ransomed him from the sacrifice, and the good news of prophethood was not at his birth."* [Tafsir al-Tabari (23/57).]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father told us, Abu Nu'aym told us, Sufyan al-Thawri told us, from Dawud, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾, he said: "He was given good news of him when he was born, and when he was made a prophet."

Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah said, from Qatadah, concerning His words: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾, he said: "After what had happened with him, when he surrendered himself to Allah, and Allah said: ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac﴾."

* *

His words: ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are those who do good and those who clearly wrong themselves﴾ are like His words, Exalted: ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend in peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations [descended] from those with you. And there will be nations We will grant enjoyment; then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾ [Hud 11:48].

Allah, exalted is He, says, informing about His friend Ibrahim (peace be upon him) [addition from manuscripts T and S]: After Allah had given him victory over his people, and after he had despaired of their faith having witnessed the great signs, he emigrated from among them and said: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me. My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ That is, he asked for obedient children as a replacement for his people and kindred whom he had left. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾ This boy was Isma'il (peace be upon him), for he was the first son whose birth Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was given good tidings of. He was older than Ishaq by the consensus of the Muslims and the People of the Book. Indeed, in the text of their own scripture it is stated that Isma'il was born to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) when he was eighty-six years old, and that Ishaq was born when Ibrahim was ninety-nine years old. According to them, Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice his son, his only son, and in one version, "his firstborn." So they inserted here, falsely and with slander, "Ishaq." This is not permissible, because it contradicts the text of their scripture. They inserted "Ishaq" only because he is their father, whereas Isma'il is the father of the Arabs, so they envied them. They added to it and distorted the word "only son" (wahid), giving it the meaning of "the one who has no other," since Isma'il had been taken by his father, together with his mother, to the area beside Makkah. This is a false interpretation and a baseless distortion, for the word "wahid" is only used of one who has no other. Moreover, the firstborn son has a distinction that later sons do not have, so the command to sacrifice him is more emphatic as a trial and test.

A group of scholars held that the one sacrificed was Ishaq. This view is attributed to a group of the early generations (al-salaf), and it is even reported from some of the Companions (al-Sahabah). But it is not found in the Book or the Sunnah. I do not think this view was taken except from the rabbis of the People of the Book, and it was accepted as settled without evidence. The Book of Allah bears witness to and guides toward its being Isma'il, for it mentions the good tidings of the forbearing boy and mentions that he is the one to be sacrificed. Then after that He said: ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ When the angels gave Ibrahim good tidings of Ishaq, they said: ﴿Indeed, we give you good tidings of a knowing boy.﴾ [al-Hijr: 53] And He said: ﴿So We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub.﴾ [Hud: 71] That is, a son named Ya'qub would be born to him during the lifetime of both of them, and from his offspring would come descendants and progeny. We have already mentioned there that after this promise it is not permissible that he be commanded to sacrifice him while still a child, because Allah [the Exalted] [addition in manuscript T] had promised both of them that he would have descendants and that there would be progeny for him. How, then, could he be commanded to sacrifice him as a child after this? Isma'il is described here as forbearing because that suits this situation.

* *

His saying: ﴿When he reached the age of exertion with him⟩ means: he grew up, became strong, and began to walk with his father and go about with him. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used to go at all times to check on his son and the son's mother in the land of Faran, and to look into their affairs. It has been mentioned that he would ride swiftly to that place on the Buraq. But Allah knows best.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata al-Khurasani, Zayd ibn Aslam, and others: ﴿When he reached the age of exertion with him⟩ means: he grew up, became capable, and was able to do what his father did of striving and working. ﴿When he reached the age of exertion with him, he said: "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think."⟩ 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: The dreams of the prophets are revelation. Then he recited this verse: ﴿He said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think."⟩

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated to us: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn al-Junayd narrated to us, Abu 'Abd al-Malik al-Karandi narrated to us, Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from Isra'il ibn Yunus, from Simak, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dreams of the prophets in sleep are revelation." This is not in any of the Six Books by this route. [Al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (12/6) narrated it by another route from Simak: he narrated it through al-Firyabi, from Sufyan, from Simak ibn Harb, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas.]

He informed his son of this only so that it would be easier for him, and to test his patience, endurance, and resolve from his youth in obeying Allah the Exalted and obeying his father.

﴿He said, "O my father, do what you are commanded."⟩ That is: carry out what Allah has commanded you regarding my slaughter. ﴿"You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient."⟩ That is: I will be patient and will seek reward for that with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He spoke the truth, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, in what he promised. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet. And he used to enjoin on his people prayer and zakah, and he was pleasing to his Lord.⟩ [Maryam: 54–55]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when they both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead⟩ means: when both of them bore witness [to the faith] and remembered Allah the Exalted, Ibrahim [prepared] for the slaughter, and the son [prepared] for the witness of death. It is also said: ﴿aslama﴾ [in the sense] of [yastaslima] and yanqada: they surrendered and submitted. Ibrahim complied with Allah's command, and Isma'il obeyed Allah and his father. This was said by Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Ibn Ishaq, and others.

The meaning of ﴿and he put him down upon his forehead⟩ is that he threw him onto his face so that he could slaughter him from the nape of his neck, and so that he would not see his face at the time of slaughter, to make it easier for him. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, and Qatadah said: ﴿and he put him down upon his forehead⟩ means: he laid him down on his face.

Imam Ahmad said: Surayj [in manuscript A: Shurayj] and Yunus narrated to us, both saying: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Abu 'Asim al-Ghanawi, from Abu al-Tufayl [in manuscript T: "with its chain"], from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: When Ibrahim was commanded with the rites (al-manasik) [in manuscript A: "When Allah commanded Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with the rites"], Satan confronted him at the place of running (al-sa'y), so he raced him, and Ibrahim outran him. Then Jibril took him to Jamrat al-'Aqabah, and Satan confronted him there, so he pelted him with seven pebbles until he departed. Then he confronted him at the middle jamrah, and he pelted him with seven pebbles. Then he laid him down upon his forehead, and Isma'il was wearing a white shirt. He said to him: "O father, I have no garment to be shrouded in except this one, so take it off so that you may shroud me in it." He began to take it off, and he was called from behind: ﴿"O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision."⟩ Ibrahim turned, and behold, there was a white ram with curled horns and beautiful eyes. Ibn 'Abbas said: We used to follow that kind of ram.

He mentioned the complete hadith at length in "al-Manasik." [al-Musnad (1/297)] Then Ahmad narrated it at length from Yunus, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from 'Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr [in manuscript T: "with its chain"], from Ibn 'Abbas, and he mentioned something similar, except that he said: "Ishaq." [al-Musnad (1/306)] So there are two reports from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the identity of the one to be sacrificed, and the more apparent from him is Isma'il, for reasons that will come later.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, from al-Hasan ibn Dinar, from Qatadah, from Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.⟩ He said: A ram came out to him from Paradise, which had grazed for forty autumns before that. Ibrahim sent his son away and followed the ram, and it led him to the first jamrah, and he pelted it with seven pebbles, and it escaped from him there. It came to the middle jamrah, and he brought it out there, and he pelted it with seven pebbles, and then it escaped. He caught up with it at the greatest jamrah, and he pelted it with seven pebbles, and brought it out there. Then he took it and brought it to the place of sacrifice (al-manhar) at Mina, and slaughtered it. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Ibn 'Abbas, the head of the ram was indeed hanging by its horns on the gutter of the Ka'bah from the beginning of Islam, and it had dried out, meaning: it had become dry.

'Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, who informed us, al-Qasim said: Abu Hurayrah and Ka'b met. Abu Hurayrah began to narrate from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ka'b began to narrate from the scriptures. Abu Hurayrah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every prophet has a supplication that is answered, and I have kept my supplication as an intercession for my nation on the Day of Resurrection." Ka'b said to him: "Did you hear this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "Yes." He said: "May my father and mother be your ransom, or: may his father and mother be his ransom. Shall I not tell you about Ibrahim (peace be upon him)? When he was shown the sacrifice of his son Ishaq, Satan said: 'If I do not tempt these people at this [moment], I will never tempt them.' So Ibrahim went out with his son to sacrifice him. Satan went and entered upon Sarah and said: 'Where did Ibrahim take your son?' She said: 'He went out with him for some need of his.' He said: 'He did not go out for a need; he took him only to sacrifice him.' She said: 'And why would he sacrifice him?' He said: 'He claims that his Lord commanded him to do so.' She said: 'Then he has done well to obey his Lord.' Satan went after the two of them and said to the boy: 'Where is your father taking you?' He said: 'For some need of his.' He said: 'He does not take you for a need; he takes you only to sacrifice you.' He said: 'And why would he sacrifice me?' He said: 'He claims that his Lord commanded him to do so.' He said: 'By Allah, if Allah has commanded him to do so, then he will certainly do it.' So he despaired of him, and he left him and caught up with Ibrahim, and said: 'Where did you go out with your son?' He said: 'For a need.' He said: 'You did not go out with him for a need; you went out with him only to sacrifice him.' He said: 'And why would I sacrifice him?' He said: 'You claim that your Lord commanded you to do so.' He said: 'By Allah, if my Lord has commanded me to do so, I will certainly do it.' So he left him and despaired of being obeyed."

Ibn Jarir narrated it from Yunus, from Ibn Wahb, from Yunus ibn Yazid, from Ibn Shihab, that 'Amr ibn Abi Sufyan ibn Usayd [in manuscript A: "Asad"] ibn Jariyah al-Thaqafi informed him that Ka'b said to Abu Hurayrah ... and he mentioned it at length, and at its end he said: Allah revealed to Ishaq: "I have given you a supplication, and I will answer you in it." Ishaq said: "O Allah, I ask You to accept from me: any servant who meets You from among the first and the last, who does not associate anything with You, admit him into Paradise."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated to us: My father narrated to us, Muhammad ibn al-Wazir al-Dimashqi narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam narrated to us, from his father, from 'Ata ibn Yasar [in manuscript T: "and he narrated with his chain"], from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) [addition from manuscript T], who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah gave me the choice between forgiving half of my nation and between my keeping my intercession hidden. So I hid my intercession, and I hoped that it would be [an expiation] for my nation as a whole [in manuscript A: 'that it would be more general']. And had it not been for what the righteous servant (Ibrahim) had preceded me in, I would have hastened my supplication for it. Indeed, when Allah relieved Ishaq of the distress of the slaughter, it was said to him: 'O Ishaq, ask, and you will be given.' He said: 'As for Him in whose hand is my soul, I will hasten it before the whisperings of Satan. O Allah, whoever dies without associating anything with You, forgive him and admit him into Paradise.'"

This is a hadith, a strange and rejected (munkar) narration, narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Awsat (no. 3603) and by Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil (4/272) through al-Walid ibn Muslim, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, with it. Ibn Abi Hatim also mentioned it in al-'Ilal (2/219) and said: "I asked my father, and he said: 'This is a munkar hadith.'" 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam is weak in narration. I fear that there is an interpolated addition (mudraja) in the hadith, namely his saying: "Indeed Allah, when He relieved Ishaq..." to the end. And Allah knows best. So if this is preserved, the more likely reading is that the context is about Isma'il, and they distorted it to Ishaq out of envy, as has already been mentioned. Otherwise, the rites of pilgrimage and the sacrifices are only located at Mina, in the land of Makkah, where Isma'il, not Ishaq, was [peace be upon them both]. Ishaq was in the land of Canaan in the region of the Levant.

* *

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ That is: the purpose of your vision has been achieved by your laying your son down for slaughter.

Al-Suddi and others mentioned that he drew the knife across his neck, but it did not cut anything; rather, a plate of copper came between the knife and him. Then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was called at that moment: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision.﴾

* *

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ That is: thus do We turn away from those who obey Us hardships and calamities, and We make for them, in their affair, relief and a way out, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Allah has already set for everything a decree.﴾ [At-Talaq: 2-3]

A group of scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) used this verse and the story as evidence for the validity of naskh (abrogation, the lifting of a previously prescribed ruling by a later one) before the command could be carried out, contrary to a group of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school). The proof from this is clear: Allah the Exalted prescribed for Ibrahim the slaughter of his son, then abrogated it for him and turned it into a ransom. The primary purpose of the original command was to reward the Friend (Khalil) for his patience in the face of slaughtering his son and his determination to do so. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial.﴾ That is: the evident and manifest test, in that he was commanded to slaughter his son, and he hastened to that, submitting to the command of Allah and obeying Him. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant].﴾ [An-Najm: 37]

* *

And His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ Sufyan al-Thawri narrated from Jabir al-Ju'fi, from Abu al-Tufayl, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾: he said: "With a white ram, with beautiful eyes and curved horns, which had been tied to a samurah tree." Abu al-Tufayl said: "They found it tied to a samurah tree on Thabir."

Al-Thawri also said, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman ibn Khuthaym, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A ram that had grazed in Paradise for forty autumns."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Saffar narrated to us, Dawud al-'Attar narrated to us, from Ibn Khuthaym, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The rock that is in Mina at the base of Thabir is the rock on which Ibrahim slaughtered the ransom for his son. There descended upon it from Thabir a ram, with beautiful eyes and curved horns, which bleated; so he slaughtered it. It is the ram that Adam's son (Qabil/Habil) offered, and it was accepted from him. It was kept stored until Ishaq was ransomed with it."

It is also narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "The ram used to graze in Paradise until Thabir split open for it, and it had red wool on it."

From al-Hasan al-Basri: the name of Ibrahim's ram was Jarir.

Ibn Jurayj said: 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "He slaughtered it at al-Maqam." Mujahid said: "He slaughtered it at Mina, at the place of sacrifice (al-mantar)." Hushaym narrated from Sayyar, from 'Ikrimah, that Ibn 'Abbas once issued a fatwa to the one who had vowed to sacrifice himself, instructing him to sacrifice one hundred camels. Then he said afterwards: "Had I issued him a fatwa to sacrifice a ram, it would have sufficed him to slaughter a ram, for Allah the Exalted said in His Book: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾" The sound view, which most scholars hold, is that he was ransomed with a ram. Al-Thawri narrated from a man, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾: he said: "A wa'l (a mountain goat)."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, from al-Hasan, that he used to say: "Isma'il was ransomed only with a male antelope (tays min al-aruwa), which descended upon him from Thabir."

Imam Ahmad has also said: Sufyan narrated to us, Mansur narrated to us, from his maternal uncle Musafi', from Safiyyah bint Shaybah, who said: "A woman from the Banu Sulaym, who had given birth to most of the people of our household, informed me that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent for 'Uthman ibn Talhah" (and at one point she said: "She asked 'Uthman: 'Why did the Prophet ﷺ call you?' He said: 'He said: "I had seen the two horns of the ram when I entered the House, and I forgot to order you to cover them. So cover them, for it is not fitting that there be anything in the House that distracts the one who prays."'") Sufyan said: "The two horns of the ram remained hanging in the House until the House burned, and they burned." [Al-Musnad (4/68)]

This is independent evidence that it was Isma'il, peace be upon him, for the Quraysh inherited the two horns of the ram with which Ibrahim was ransomed, from predecessor to successor, generation after generation, until Allah sent His Messenger ﷺ.

A section on the narrations transmitted from the early generations (al-salaf) regarding who the sacrificed son was:

Mention of those who said: it was Ishaq [peace be upon him]:

Hamzah al-Zayyat narrated from Abu Maysarah, may Allah have mercy on him, who said: Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to the king to his face: "Do you desire to eat with me? I am—by Allah—Yusuf ibn Ya'qub, the Prophet of Allah, son of Ishaq, the one who was sacrificed by Allah, son of Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah."

Al-Thawri said, from Abu Sinan, from Ibn Abi al-Hudhayl: that Yusuf, peace be upon him, said the same to the king.

Sufyan al-Thawri said, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, from his father, who said: "Musa said: 'O Lord, they say: "O God of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub." Why do they say that?' He said: 'Ibrahim never once preferred anything over Me without My choosing him over it. As for Ishaq, he gave himself to Me for slaughter, and he was more generous than that. As for Ya'qub, whenever I increased him in trial, he increased in good opinion of Me.'"

Shu'bah said, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, who said: A man boasted in the presence of Ibn Mas'ud, saying: "I am so-and-so son of so-and-so, the son of noble elders." 'Abd Allah said: "That is Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq, the one sacrificed by Allah, son of Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah [may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all]."

This is sound up to Ibn Mas'ud. Likewise, 'Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was Ishaq, and from his father al-'Abbas and from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib the same. Likewise said 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Abu Maysarah, Zayd ibn Aslam, 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, al-Zuhri, al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, Makhul, 'Uthman ibn Hadir, al-Suddi, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu al-Hudhayl, and Ibn Sabit. This is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir. His narration from Ka'b al-Ahbar that it was Ishaq has already been mentioned.

Thus Ibn Ishaq narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Sufyan ibn al-'Ala', ibn Jariyah, from Abu Hurayrah, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, that he said: "It was Ishaq." [Narrated by al-Tabari in his tafsir (23/52)]

And all of these reports, and Allah knows best, derive from Ka'b al-Ahbar. For when he embraced Islam during the caliphate of 'Umar, he began to narrate to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, from his books. 'Umar would sometimes listen to him, so people became lenient about listening to what he had, and they transmitted from him both its worthless and its valuable parts, while this Ummah—and Allah knows best—has no need for a single letter of what he had. Al-Baghawi has recorded this view, that it was Ishaq, from 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, and al-'Abbas, and from the Successors (tabi'un): Ka'b al-Ahbar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Masruq, 'Ikrimah, Muqatil, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, and al-Suddi. He said: "And it is one of the two reports from Ibn 'Abbas." [Ma'alim al-Tanzil of al-Baghawi (7/46)]

A hadith has been transmitted on this subject—if it were established, we would act upon it wholeheartedly, but its chain is not sound. Ibn Jarir said:

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, Zayd ibn Hubab narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Dinar, from 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, from al-Hasan, from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, from the Prophet ﷺ, in a hadith he mentioned, who said: "He was Ishaq." [Tafsir al-Tabari (23/52)]

In its chain there are two weak narrators: al-Hasan ibn Dinar al-Basri, who is abandoned (matruk), and 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, whose narrations are munkar. Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it from his father, from Muslim ibn Ibrahim, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, with it, raised to the Prophet ﷺ, and that he said: "He was Ishaq." Then he said: "It was also narrated by Mubarak ibn Fadalah, from al-Hasan, from al-Ahnaf, from al-'Abbas, as his own statement (mawquf), and this is more likely and more sound."

[Mention of the reports stating that it was Isma'il, peace be upon him, which is the sound and definitive view]

The narration from Ibn 'Abbas that it was Ishaq has already been mentioned. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Amir al-Sha'bi, Yusuf ibn Mihran, Mujahid, 'Ata', and others said, from Ibn 'Abbas, that it was Isma'il, peace be upon him.

Ibn Jarir said: Yunus narrated to me, Ibn Wahb informed us, 'Amr ibn Qays informed me, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "The one ransomed was Isma'il, peace be upon him. The Jews claim that it was Ishaq, but the Jews are lying." [Tafsir al-Tabari (23/52)]

Israil narrated from Thawr, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The sacrificed one was Isma'il."

Ibn Abi Najih said, from Mujahid: "It was Isma'il." Yusuf ibn Mihran also said the same.

Al-Sha'bi said: "It was Isma'il, peace be upon him, and I have seen the two horns of the ram in the Ka'bah."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from al-Hasan ibn Dinar and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, from al-Hasan al-Basri, that he had no doubt about this: that the one of Ibrahim's two sons he was commanded to sacrifice was Isma'il.

Ibn Ishaq said: "I heard Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi say: 'The one whom Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice from among his two sons was Isma'il. We find that in the Book of Allah, for when Allah finished the story of the one sacrificed from Ibrahim's two sons, He said: ﴿And We gave him good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ Allah says: ﴿So We gave her good news of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub.﴾ That means: a son and a grandson. So He would not have commanded him to sacrifice Ishaq when He had promised him through him what He promised. The one He commanded to be sacrificed was none other than Isma'il.'"

Ibn Ishaq said, on the authority of Buraydah ibn Sufyan ibn Farwah al-Aslami, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, that he [Muhammad ibn Ka'b] told them that he mentioned this to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz when he was caliph and [Muhammad] was with him in al-Sham. Umar said to him, "This is a matter I had never considered, and I indeed see it as you have said." Then he sent for a man who was with him in al-Sham, who had been a Jew, then embraced Islam and whose Islam was good, and who thought of himself as one of their scholars. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asked him about this. (Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "I was with Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz.") Umar said to him, "Which of Abraham's two sons was he commanded to sacrifice?" He said, "Isma'il, by Allah, O Commander of the Faithful. The Jews indeed know this, but they envy you, the Arab people, that your father is the one to whom this occurred by the command of Allah, and the virtue Allah mentioned of him for his patience in what he was commanded. So they deny it and claim it was Isaac, because Isaac is their father. Allah knows best which of them it was. Both were pure, good, and obedient to Allah, Mighty and Majestic."* [Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (23/54).]

'Abd Allah ibn al-Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "I asked my father about the one who was sacrificed: who was he? Isma'il or Isaac?" He said, "Isma'il." He mentioned this in the Kitab al-Zuhd (Book of Asceticism).

Ibn Abi Hatim said: "And I heard my father say: 'The correct view is that the one sacrificed was Isma'il, peace be upon him.'" He said: "It is also reported from Ali, Ibn Umar, Abu Hurayrah, Abu al-Tufayl, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali, and Abu Salih, that they said: 'The one sacrificed was Isma'il.'"

Al-Baghawi said in his Tafsir: "This is the view of Abd Allah ibn Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Suddi, al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and al-Kalbi. It is also a narration from Ibn Abbas. He also reported it from Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala'."* [Ma'alim al-Tanzil of al-Baghawi (7/47).]

Ibn Jarir narrated a strange hadith on this. He said: Muhammad ibn Ammar al-Razi told me, Isma'il ibn Ubayd ibn Abi Karimah told us, Umar ibn Abd al-Rahim al-Khattabi told us, from Ubayd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Utbi (a descendant of Utbah ibn Abi Sufyan), from his father, who said: Abd Allah ibn Sa'id told me, from al-Sunabihi, who said: "We were with Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, and the people mentioned the sacrificed one: Isma'il or Isaac? He said: 'You have fallen into [a matter] of which the knowledgeable one knows. We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when a man came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, give me from what Allah has granted you, O son of the two sacrificed ones!" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ laughed. It was said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, who are the two sacrificed ones?" He said: "When Abd al-Muttalib was commanded to dig Zamzam, he vowed to Allah that if Allah made its matter easy for him, he would sacrifice one of his sons. The arrow fell upon Abd Allah, but his maternal uncles prevented it and said: 'Ransom your son with a hundred camels.' So he ransomed him with a hundred camels. The second [sacrificed one] was Isma'il.'"*[Tafsir al-Tabari (23/54).]

This is a very strange hadith. Al-Umawi also narrated it in his Maghazi: some of our companions told us, Isma'il ibn Ubayd ibn Abi Karimah informed us, Umar ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Qurashi told us, Ubayd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Utbi (a descendant of Utbah ibn Abi Sufyan) told us, Abd Allah ibn Sa'id told us, al-Sunabihi told us, who said: "We attended the gathering of Mu'awiyah, and the people discussed Isma'il and Isaac," and he mentioned it. So I copied it this way from a faulty copy [in the text: "from a copy of such-and-such, and Allah knows best"].

Ibn Jarir based his preference that the sacrificed one was Isaac on the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾. He took this good news to be the good news of Isaac in the words: ﴿And they gave him good news of a knowing boy﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:28]. He answered the good news of Ya'qub (Jacob) by saying that he had reached the age of striving with him, meaning working. It is possible that children had also been born to him with Ya'qub. He said: As for the two horns that were hanging in the Ka'bah, it is permissible that they were brought from the lands of al-Sham. He said: It has already been mentioned that some people held that he sacrificed Isaac there. This is what he relied upon in his Tafsir, but what he held is neither a sound doctrine nor a binding one; rather it is very far-fetched. What Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi used as evidence that it was Isma'il is more firmly established, more sound, and stronger. Allah knows best.* [Imam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, examined this issue in his Fatawa. See the references in the General Index (36/32).]

* *

His words: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. Since the good news of the sacrificed one, who is Isma'il, was mentioned earlier, He followed it with the mention of the good news of his brother Isaac. I have mentioned this in the commentary on Surah Hud and Surah al-Hijr.* [Surah Hud, verse 71; Surah al-Hijr, verse 53.]

* *

His words: ﴿nabiyyan﴾ (a prophet) is a circumstantial clause (hal) that is anticipated, meaning: a prophet from among the righteous will come from him.

Ibn Jarir said: Ya'qub told me, Ibn Ulayyah told us, from Dawud, from Ikrimah, who said: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The sacrificed one was Isaac." He said: As for His words, ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾, he said: "He gave him good news of his prophethood." He said: As for His words, ﴿And We bestowed upon him out of Our mercy his brother Aaron, a prophet﴾ [Maryam 19:53], he said: "Aaron was older than Musa, but the meaning is: He granted him his prophethood."

And Ibn Abd al-A'la told us, al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman told us, he said: "I heard Dawud narrate, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, concerning this verse: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾," he said: "He gave him good news of him as a prophet only when Allah ransomed him from the sacrifice, and the good news of prophethood was not at his birth."* [Tafsir al-Tabari (23/57).]

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father told us, Abu Nu'aym told us, Sufyan al-Thawri told us, from Dawud, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾, he said: "He was given good news of him when he was born, and when he was made a prophet."

Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah said, from Qatadah, concerning His words: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾, he said: "After what had happened with him, when he surrendered himself to Allah, and Allah said: ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac﴾."

* *

His words: ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are those who do good and those who clearly wrong themselves﴾ are like His words, Exalted: ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend in peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations [descended] from those with you. And there will be nations We will grant enjoyment; then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾ [Hud 11:48].

Allah, exalted is He, says, informing about His friend Ibrahim (peace be upon him) [addition from manuscripts T and S]: After Allah had given him victory over his people, and after he had despaired of their faith having witnessed the great signs, he emigrated from among them and said: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me. My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ That is, he asked for obedient children as a replacement for his people and kindred whom he had left. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾ This boy was Isma'il (peace be upon him), for he was the first son whose birth Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was given good tidings of. He was older than Ishaq by the consensus of the Muslims and the People of the Book. Indeed, in the text of their own scripture it is stated that Isma'il was born to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) when he was eighty-six years old, and that Ishaq was born when Ibrahim was ninety-nine years old. According to them, Allah commanded Ibrahim to sacrifice his son, his only son, and in one version, "his firstborn." So they inserted here, falsely and with slander, "Ishaq." This is not permissible, because it contradicts the text of their scripture. They inserted "Ishaq" only because he is their father, whereas Isma'il is the father of the Arabs, so they envied them. They added to it and distorted the word "only son" (wahid), giving it the meaning of "the one who has no other," since Isma'il had been taken by his father, together with his mother, to the area beside Makkah. This is a false interpretation and a baseless distortion, for the word "wahid" is only used of one who has no other. Moreover, the firstborn son has a distinction that later sons do not have, so the command to sacrifice him is more emphatic as a trial and test.

A group of scholars held that the one sacrificed was Ishaq. This view is attributed to a group of the early generations (al-salaf), and it is even reported from some of the Companions (al-Sahabah). But it is not found in the Book or the Sunnah. I do not think this view was taken except from the rabbis of the People of the Book, and it was accepted as settled without evidence. The Book of Allah bears witness to and guides toward its being Isma'il, for it mentions the good tidings of the forbearing boy and mentions that he is the one to be sacrificed. Then after that He said: ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ When the angels gave Ibrahim good tidings of Ishaq, they said: ﴿Indeed, we give you good tidings of a knowing boy.﴾ [al-Hijr: 53] And He said: ﴿So We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub.﴾ [Hud: 71] That is, a son named Ya'qub would be born to him during the lifetime of both of them, and from his offspring would come descendants and progeny. We have already mentioned there that after this promise it is not permissible that he be commanded to sacrifice him while still a child, because Allah [the Exalted] [addition in manuscript T] had promised both of them that he would have descendants and that there would be progeny for him. How, then, could he be commanded to sacrifice him as a child after this? Isma'il is described here as forbearing because that suits this situation.

* *

His saying: ﴿When he reached the age of exertion with him⟩ means: he grew up, became strong, and began to walk with his father and go about with him. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used to go at all times to check on his son and the son's mother in the land of Faran, and to look into their affairs. It has been mentioned that he would ride swiftly to that place on the Buraq. But Allah knows best.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata al-Khurasani, Zayd ibn Aslam, and others: ﴿When he reached the age of exertion with him⟩ means: he grew up, became capable, and was able to do what his father did of striving and working. ﴿When he reached the age of exertion with him, he said: "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think."⟩ 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: The dreams of the prophets are revelation. Then he recited this verse: ﴿He said, "O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think."⟩

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated to us: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn al-Junayd narrated to us, Abu 'Abd al-Malik al-Karandi narrated to us, Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from Isra'il ibn Yunus, from Simak, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dreams of the prophets in sleep are revelation." This is not in any of the Six Books by this route. [Al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (12/6) narrated it by another route from Simak: he narrated it through al-Firyabi, from Sufyan, from Simak ibn Harb, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas.]

He informed his son of this only so that it would be easier for him, and to test his patience, endurance, and resolve from his youth in obeying Allah the Exalted and obeying his father.

﴿He said, "O my father, do what you are commanded."⟩ That is: carry out what Allah has commanded you regarding my slaughter. ﴿"You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient."⟩ That is: I will be patient and will seek reward for that with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He spoke the truth, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, in what he promised. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet. And he used to enjoin on his people prayer and zakah, and he was pleasing to his Lord.⟩ [Maryam: 54–55]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when they both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead⟩ means: when both of them bore witness [to the faith] and remembered Allah the Exalted, Ibrahim [prepared] for the slaughter, and the son [prepared] for the witness of death. It is also said: ﴿aslama﴾ [in the sense] of [yastaslima] and yanqada: they surrendered and submitted. Ibrahim complied with Allah's command, and Isma'il obeyed Allah and his father. This was said by Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Ibn Ishaq, and others.

The meaning of ﴿and he put him down upon his forehead⟩ is that he threw him onto his face so that he could slaughter him from the nape of his neck, and so that he would not see his face at the time of slaughter, to make it easier for him. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, and Qatadah said: ﴿and he put him down upon his forehead⟩ means: he laid him down on his face.

Imam Ahmad said: Surayj [in manuscript A: Shurayj] and Yunus narrated to us, both saying: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Abu 'Asim al-Ghanawi, from Abu al-Tufayl [in manuscript T: "with its chain"], from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: When Ibrahim was commanded with the rites (al-manasik) [in manuscript A: "When Allah commanded Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with the rites"], Satan confronted him at the place of running (al-sa'y), so he raced him, and Ibrahim outran him. Then Jibril took him to Jamrat al-'Aqabah, and Satan confronted him there, so he pelted him with seven pebbles until he departed. Then he confronted him at the middle jamrah, and he pelted him with seven pebbles. Then he laid him down upon his forehead, and Isma'il was wearing a white shirt. He said to him: "O father, I have no garment to be shrouded in except this one, so take it off so that you may shroud me in it." He began to take it off, and he was called from behind: ﴿"O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision."⟩ Ibrahim turned, and behold, there was a white ram with curled horns and beautiful eyes. Ibn 'Abbas said: We used to follow that kind of ram.

He mentioned the complete hadith at length in "al-Manasik." [al-Musnad (1/297)] Then Ahmad narrated it at length from Yunus, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from 'Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr [in manuscript T: "with its chain"], from Ibn 'Abbas, and he mentioned something similar, except that he said: "Ishaq." [al-Musnad (1/306)] So there are two reports from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the identity of the one to be sacrificed, and the more apparent from him is Isma'il, for reasons that will come later.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, from al-Hasan ibn Dinar, from Qatadah, from Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.⟩ He said: A ram came out to him from Paradise, which had grazed for forty autumns before that. Ibrahim sent his son away and followed the ram, and it led him to the first jamrah, and he pelted it with seven pebbles, and it escaped from him there. It came to the middle jamrah, and he brought it out there, and he pelted it with seven pebbles, and then it escaped. He caught up with it at the greatest jamrah, and he pelted it with seven pebbles, and brought it out there. Then he took it and brought it to the place of sacrifice (al-manhar) at Mina, and slaughtered it. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Ibn 'Abbas, the head of the ram was indeed hanging by its horns on the gutter of the Ka'bah from the beginning of Islam, and it had dried out, meaning: it had become dry.

'Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, who informed us, al-Qasim said: Abu Hurayrah and Ka'b met. Abu Hurayrah began to narrate from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ka'b began to narrate from the scriptures. Abu Hurayrah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every prophet has a supplication that is answered, and I have kept my supplication as an intercession for my nation on the Day of Resurrection." Ka'b said to him: "Did you hear this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "Yes." He said: "May my father and mother be your ransom, or: may his father and mother be his ransom. Shall I not tell you about Ibrahim (peace be upon him)? When he was shown the sacrifice of his son Ishaq, Satan said: 'If I do not tempt these people at this [moment], I will never tempt them.' So Ibrahim went out with his son to sacrifice him. Satan went and entered upon Sarah and said: 'Where did Ibrahim take your son?' She said: 'He went out with him for some need of his.' He said: 'He did not go out for a need; he took him only to sacrifice him.' She said: 'And why would he sacrifice him?' He said: 'He claims that his Lord commanded him to do so.' She said: 'Then he has done well to obey his Lord.' Satan went after the two of them and said to the boy: 'Where is your father taking you?' He said: 'For some need of his.' He said: 'He does not take you for a need; he takes you only to sacrifice you.' He said: 'And why would he sacrifice me?' He said: 'He claims that his Lord commanded him to do so.' He said: 'By Allah, if Allah has commanded him to do so, then he will certainly do it.' So he despaired of him, and he left him and caught up with Ibrahim, and said: 'Where did you go out with your son?' He said: 'For a need.' He said: 'You did not go out with him for a need; you went out with him only to sacrifice him.' He said: 'And why would I sacrifice him?' He said: 'You claim that your Lord commanded you to do so.' He said: 'By Allah, if my Lord has commanded me to do so, I will certainly do it.' So he left him and despaired of being obeyed."

Ibn Jarir narrated it from Yunus, from Ibn Wahb, from Yunus ibn Yazid, from Ibn Shihab, that 'Amr ibn Abi Sufyan ibn Usayd [in manuscript A: "Asad"] ibn Jariyah al-Thaqafi informed him that Ka'b said to Abu Hurayrah ... and he mentioned it at length, and at its end he said: Allah revealed to Ishaq: "I have given you a supplication, and I will answer you in it." Ishaq said: "O Allah, I ask You to accept from me: any servant who meets You from among the first and the last, who does not associate anything with You, admit him into Paradise."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated to us: My father narrated to us, Muhammad ibn al-Wazir al-Dimashqi narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam narrated to us, from his father, from 'Ata ibn Yasar [in manuscript T: "and he narrated with his chain"], from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) [addition from manuscript T], who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah gave me the choice between forgiving half of my nation and between my keeping my intercession hidden. So I hid my intercession, and I hoped that it would be [an expiation] for my nation as a whole [in manuscript A: 'that it would be more general']. And had it not been for what the righteous servant (Ibrahim) had preceded me in, I would have hastened my supplication for it. Indeed, when Allah relieved Ishaq of the distress of the slaughter, it was said to him: 'O Ishaq, ask, and you will be given.' He said: 'As for Him in whose hand is my soul, I will hasten it before the whisperings of Satan. O Allah, whoever dies without associating anything with You, forgive him and admit him into Paradise.'"

This is a hadith, a strange and rejected (munkar) narration, narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Awsat (no. 3603) and by Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil (4/272) through al-Walid ibn Muslim, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, with it. Ibn Abi Hatim also mentioned it in al-'Ilal (2/219) and said: "I asked my father, and he said: 'This is a munkar hadith.'" 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam is weak in narration. I fear that there is an interpolated addition (mudraja) in the hadith, namely his saying: "Indeed Allah, when He relieved Ishaq..." to the end. And Allah knows best. So if this is preserved, the more likely reading is that the context is about Isma'il, and they distorted it to Ishaq out of envy, as has already been mentioned. Otherwise, the rites of pilgrimage and the sacrifices are only located at Mina, in the land of Makkah, where Isma'il, not Ishaq, was [peace be upon them both]. Ishaq was in the land of Canaan in the region of the Levant.

* *

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision."﴾ That is: the purpose of your vision has been achieved by your laying your son down for slaughter.

Al-Suddi and others mentioned that he drew the knife across his neck, but it did not cut anything; rather, a plate of copper came between the knife and him. Then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was called at that moment: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision.﴾

* *

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ That is: thus do We turn away from those who obey Us hardships and calamities, and We make for them, in their affair, relief and a way out, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Allah has already set for everything a decree.﴾ [At-Talaq: 2-3]

A group of scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) used this verse and the story as evidence for the validity of naskh (abrogation, the lifting of a previously prescribed ruling by a later one) before the command could be carried out, contrary to a group of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school). The proof from this is clear: Allah the Exalted prescribed for Ibrahim the slaughter of his son, then abrogated it for him and turned it into a ransom. The primary purpose of the original command was to reward the Friend (Khalil) for his patience in the face of slaughtering his son and his determination to do so. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial.﴾ That is: the evident and manifest test, in that he was commanded to slaughter his son, and he hastened to that, submitting to the command of Allah and obeying Him. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant].﴾ [An-Najm: 37]

* *

And His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ Sufyan al-Thawri narrated from Jabir al-Ju'fi, from Abu al-Tufayl, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾: he said: "With a white ram, with beautiful eyes and curved horns, which had been tied to a samurah tree." Abu al-Tufayl said: "They found it tied to a samurah tree on Thabir."

Al-Thawri also said, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman ibn Khuthaym, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A ram that had grazed in Paradise for forty autumns."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: My father narrated to us, Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Saffar narrated to us, Dawud al-'Attar narrated to us, from Ibn Khuthaym, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The rock that is in Mina at the base of Thabir is the rock on which Ibrahim slaughtered the ransom for his son. There descended upon it from Thabir a ram, with beautiful eyes and curved horns, which bleated; so he slaughtered it. It is the ram that Adam's son (Qabil/Habil) offered, and it was accepted from him. It was kept stored until Ishaq was ransomed with it."

It is also narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "The ram used to graze in Paradise until Thabir split open for it, and it had red wool on it."

From al-Hasan al-Basri: the name of Ibrahim's ram was Jarir.

Ibn Jurayj said: 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "He slaughtered it at al-Maqam." Mujahid said: "He slaughtered it at Mina, at the place of sacrifice (al-mantar)." Hushaym narrated from Sayyar, from 'Ikrimah, that Ibn 'Abbas once issued a fatwa to the one who had vowed to sacrifice himself, instructing him to sacrifice one hundred camels. Then he said afterwards: "Had I issued him a fatwa to sacrifice a ram, it would have sufficed him to slaughter a ram, for Allah the Exalted said in His Book: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾" The sound view, which most scholars hold, is that he was ransomed with a ram. Al-Thawri narrated from a man, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾: he said: "A wa'l (a mountain goat)."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, from al-Hasan, that he used to say: "Isma'il was ransomed only with a male antelope (tays min al-aruwa), which descended upon him from Thabir."

Imam Ahmad has also said: Sufyan narrated to us, Mansur narrated to us, from his maternal uncle Musafi', from Safiyyah bint Shaybah, who said: "A woman from the Banu Sulaym, who had given birth to most of the people of our household, informed me that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent for 'Uthman ibn Talhah" (and at one point she said: "She asked 'Uthman: 'Why did the Prophet ﷺ call you?' He said: 'He said: "I had seen the two horns of the ram when I entered the House, and I forgot to order you to cover them. So cover them, for it is not fitting that there be anything in the House that distracts the one who prays."'") Sufyan said: "The two horns of the ram remained hanging in the House until the House burned, and they burned." [Al-Musnad (4/68)]
